claims.text: Optimized cold spray deposition can produce a dense, mechanically integrated repair deposit on a damaged titanium alloy component.
Cold spray repair can eliminate hot cracking in the repaired titanium alloy region.
Cold spray can restore mechanical integrity superior to or on par with conventional fusion-weld repair.
Traditional fusion welding is ineffective for the titanium alloy component because of inherent hot-cracking risk.
The cold spray intervention can be conducted under cryogenic or room-temperature conditions.
Particle velocities of 600–800 m/s in an inert gas environment are suitable controlled parameters for the titanium repair.
Optimized surface preparation and deposition strategy ensure robust metallurgical bonding.
Mechanical interlocking and metallurgical bonding arise from severe plastic deformation of impacting powder particles.
Severe particle deformation produces an ultrafine-grained, dense deposit with minimal porosity.
The kinetic energy of high-velocity particles induces localized plastic deformation and bonding without melting.
Avoiding melting circumvents the thermal and solidification cycles that cause hot cracking.
Optimized deposition parameters produce a uniformly bonded, dense repair layer.
The repaired region will have mechanical integrity comparable to the titanium base material.
The repaired region will have thermal stability comparable to the titanium base material.
Cold spray repair will significantly reduce hot-cracking risk under aggressive operating conditions relative to fusion-weld repair.
High-temperature fusion welding can cause hot cracking and associated microstructural defects.
The repair is required to operate under aggressive aerospace or high-temperature conditions and be consistently deposited on complex component geometries.
Uniform interfacial bonding, mechanical properties across complex geometries, and process reproducibility in varied service environments remain uncertain.
